extracted.intended_audience: photojournalists, news editors, photography students, and news organizations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for editing and manipulating images used in news/photojournalism, balancing accuracy, artistic choices, and public trust. Focuses on what edits are acceptable, what constitutes manipulation, disclosure and accountability practices, and the impact of digital tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of truth / Accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Photojournalism is grounded in the principle of truth. The fundamental duty of a photojournalist is to represent events as they are, without distortion or bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accuracy is the cornerstone of journalism: present a truthful representation of the scene. Editing that alters the meaning or context of an image is considered unethical (e.g., removing an object/person, changing color to convey different mood, or cropping to exclude essential elements can alter viewer perception). Case example: Brian Walski combining two images during the Iraq War led to dismissal and damaged credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal Editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjustments to contrast, color balance, and exposure are generally acceptable as long as they don’t alter the content of the image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitted edits include contrast, color balance, and exposure adjustments; cropping is allowed but should not remove essential context or change the story the image tells. The goal is enhancing clarity and impact without altering reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding Manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Removing or adding elements, combining multiple photos, or using techniques that could deceive the viewer are strictly prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any edit that changes factual content—such as compositing separate photos, digitally adding/removing subjects, or other deceptive techniques—is unethical. Examples: Walski's composite photo; doctored Reuters images of Beirut smoke (2006); fake photos during the 2004 U.S. presidential election.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of Significant Editing
rubrics_metrics.description: If any significant editing has been done, such as altering an image for illustrative purposes, it should be clearly disclosed to the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When images are modified beyond routine corrections, media outlets should inform viewers (captions, labels, or editorial notes) to prevent misleading interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability and Editorial Review
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographers and editors should be held accountable for any unethical manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement review processes to ensure images meet ethical standards before publication; hold individuals and organizations responsible for breaches. Accountability helps protect credibility and recover public trust after incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding and Recognizing Bias in Editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Every photograph carries some level of bias; intentional manipulation of elements to support a particular narrative is unethical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of choices (angle, composition, lighting, timing) that may influence perception. Avoid selective cropping or framing that excludes essential context (e.g., cropping a protest photo to omit peaceful demonstrators and exaggerate violence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintaining Public Trust and Credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Trust is the currency of journalism; manipulating images can quickly erode this trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unethical editing harms credibility of the individual and organization and is difficult to repair. Example: Reuters retracted doctored images and suffered reputational damage; outlets should prioritize truthful representation to preserve public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing Artistic Expression with Ethical Responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Creativity is important but should never come at the cost of truth; aesthetic adjustments are acceptable if they do not distort factual content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable creative techniques include black-and-white conversion or contrast adjustments that enhance appeal without changing meaning. More drastic manipulations (digitally adding/removing elements) are unethical in news photography because they change factual content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical Use and Oversight of Digital Tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Digital editing tools make it easier to alter images, increasing the risk of unethical manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News organizations must train staff in ethical editing practices, employ software or workflows that track changes to detect potential manipulation, and remain vigilant about the consequences of even small edits on image authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Case Studies and Historical Examples to Inform Practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Examining past ethical breaches and exemplary images helps understand implications and boundaries of acceptable editing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to notable cases (TIME darkened O.J. Simpson mugshot; Syrian boy on the beach used ethically vs. later dramatized edits; fake Kerry photos from 2004) to illustrate why certain edits are problematic and to guide policy and training decisions.
